accused_occupation: Businessman/shopkeeper (as stated in the defence version)
accused_victim_relationship: Spouse (husband Manoj); Relative by marriage (father-in-law Jamnadas)
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 read with s.34; s.201; s.304-B; s.498-A
weapon: Knives and scissors were sent for examination; injuries were caused by a hard and sharp object
evidence_type: Circumstantial (primary), eyewitness (PW 1 to PW 5), medical/autopsy, forensic (blood on nails), recovery (blood stains in the house)
aggravating_circumstances: Murder inside the matrimonial house within six months of marriage; body dismembered after death and dumped in a park; crime involved more than one person
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.302 r/w s.34 IPC; life imprisonment and Rs 5,000 fine each (default one year RI); acquitted of other charges
high_court_outcome: Appeals dismissed; convictions and sentences affirmed
offence_finally_established: Murder under s.302 read with s.34 IPC
neutral_facts: The victim, a young woman, was living in her husband's family household about six months after marriage. Her body was later found cut into two pieces and wrapped in bed sheets. Blood stains were found in the family house during investigation, and samples were taken. On the evening of the incident, a group of local men saw a bundle with blood spots lying in a park, and then saw a person arrive on a scooter and throw another packet there. A police control room received a call about two blood-stained bundles in the park. The autopsy found multiple ante-mortem incised and stab injuries, including defence wounds on the hands, and post-mortem dismemberment. The medical witness stated that the injuries were caused by a hard and sharp object and that the crime could not have been committed by one person alone. Death was attributed to shock and haemorrhage from multiple injuries and was homicidal. Forensic examination found blood on the fingernail samples of one family member but not on the nails of the two accused. Knives and scissors were sent for examination. The victim's cousin identified the body. The police registered a crime against unknown persons, and a charge-sheet was later filed against the family members.
physical_harm: Death by shock and haemorrhage from twelve ante-mortem injuries; body separated into pieces post-mortem
key_evidence_accepted: Eyewitness evidence of PW 1 to PW 5 seeing the body thrown in the park; autopsy report and PW 15's testimony; blood stains in the house; forensic blood on a co-accused's nails; the false explanation given in the s.313 statements
witness_credibility: PW 1 to PW 5 accepted as proving the body was thrown in the park; PW 15 (autopsy) relied on; PW 32 declared hostile and her evidence not relied upon
post_offence_conduct: No report lodged to police about the homicidal death; false explanation given that the victim had gone to a relative's place and was missing
trial_duration: offence: 16.9.2006; trial judgment: not given (sentencing order 24.8.2009); High Court: 23.8.2012; Supreme Court: June 29, 2016
legal_representation: For appellants: Sushil Kumar Jain, Sr. Adv. (with others). For State: C. D. Singh (with others)
investigation_status: FIR/crime registered; accused arrested; charge-sheet filed against four accused; trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted under s.302/34 and life imprisonment; High Court: appeals dismissed; Supreme Court: appeals by the two appellants dismissed (mother-in-law's SLP withdrawn)
prosecution_argument: Chain of circumstances is complete; s.106 Evidence Act applies because facts were within the accused's special knowledge, so the accused had to explain the death
defence_argument: No blood found on the appellants' nails; they were at their shop during the day (alibi); no evidence against them from PW 1, 3, 4 and 5; accused has right to silence (Selvi); s.106 does not apply because prosecution did not prove presence at the house
legal_principle_applied: Five-point test for circumstantial evidence (Sharad Birdhichand Sarda); in a murder committed in secrecy inside a house, s.106 imposes a lighter but corresponding burden on the inmates to explain; a false explanation is an additional link in the chain
precedent_relied_upon: Relied on: Sharad Birdhichand Sarda v. State of Maharashtra (1984) 4 SCC 116; Trimukh Maroti Kirkan v. State of Maharashtra (2006) 10 SCC 681; Suresh v. State of Haryana (2015) 2 SCC 227; Kuldeep Singh v. State of Rajasthan (2000) 5 SCC 7; Rumi Bora Dutta v. State of Assam (2013) 7 SCC 417. Distinguished: Selvi (2010) 7 SCC 263; Tomaso Bruno (2015) 7 SCC 178; Rajkumar (2004) 12 SCC 11. Referred to: State of W.B. v. Mir Mohammad Omar (2000) 8 SCC 382; Narendra Singh (2004) 10 SCC 699
judicial_aggravating_factors: Brutal nature of the murder; body cut into pieces after death and dumped in a park; murder inside the house by more than one person
